Proto-Italic *-ājō Proto-Italic *-āō Latin -āre Vulgar Latin *accapāre Old French achever Proto-Indo-European *-mn̥ Proto-Indo-European *-mn̥tom Proto-Italic *-mentom Latin -mentum Old French -ment Old French achevement Middle French achevementbor. English achievement From Middle French achevement (compare Modern French achèvement), from Old French achevement, from the verb achever, achiever (“to finish”); equivalent to achieve + -ment. The heraldic sense may be influenced by hatchment.

senses.d: The act of achieving or performing; a successful performance; accomplishment.
ex: As to the type of seat preferred, the views were so varied that it was considered wisely that the ideal design was beyond achievement!

senses.d: A great or heroic deed or feat; something accomplished by valor or boldness.
ex: [The exploits] of the ancient saints ; they do far surpass the most famous achievements of pagan heroes.

senses.d: An escutcheon or ensign armorial; a full display or depiction of all the heraldic components to which the bearer of a coat of arms is entitled; (now especially) a funeral shield: the hatchment.
An award for completing a particular task or meeting an objective in a video game.
ex: Finishing the game does not give you a 100% score until you have unlocked all of the achievements.

senses.d: The lexical aspect (aktionsart) of verbs or predicates that change in an instant.
The successful completion of a socially defined goal or task, highlighting individual or group accomplishment.

ety.text: From réaliser + -ation.
From accomplis + -ment.
From realizzare + -zione.
From prestare + -zione. Compare Latin praestātiō (“guaranty”).
From conseguire + -mento.
Inherited from Latin lucrum. Doublet of lucro, which was borrowed. Compare English lucre.

ety.text: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese conquista, probably deverbal from conquistar. Possibly corresponds to a Vulgar Latin *conquista, from the feminine of Latin conquīsītus.

chain.g: to undertake, to embark on (an activity)

ety.text: Italian imprenderedeverb. Italian impresa Deverbal formed with the feminine past participle of imprendere, a less common alternative for intraprendere (“to undertake”). Cognate with Sicilian mprisa. Compare French entreprise for a similar construction.

chain.g: done, made, having been done or made

ety.text: From Old Galician-Portuguese feito, from Latin factum. Doublet of facto/fato.
From Old Galician-Portuguese proeza, from Old French proece, proeche, proesce (compare modern French prouesse) or Old Occitan proeza.
From Latin stemma, from Ancient Greek στέμμα (stémma).
From Middle French succes (16th c.), a borrowing from Latin successus. The verb succéder is older (13th c.).
Borrowed from Latin victōria, from vincere.

chain.g: to climb, mount or ascend, go from under; go up

ety.text: From Latin successus.

From Middle English achieven, acheven (“to accomplish (something); to acquire or obtain (something); to carry out or finish (something); to succeed in (something); to happen, turn out”), from Anglo-Norman achever, achiever, Middle French achever, achiever, and Old French achever, achiever (“to accomplish (something); to finish (something); to succeed in (something)”) (modern French achever), and then from either of the following: * Old French a- (prefix denoting addition or increase, or a change of state) + chief (“end; head”) (compare traire a chief (“to be finished”), venir a chief (“to acco…

senses.d: To carry out or conclude (something, as a task) successfully; to accomplish.
ex: Hannah achieved her lifelong dream of winning a medal at the Olympics.

senses.d: To gain or obtain (a desired objective, result, etc.) through effort or skill; to succeed in attaining (an objective, result, etc.); to win.
ex: VVhy ſome are borne great, ſome atchieue greatneſſe, and ſome haue greatneſſe throvvne vpon them.
Be it happiness or sorrow, / He postpones it till the morrow; / To the Future only cleaveth: / Nothing, therefore, he achieveth.

senses.d: To obtain (a physical thing); to get.
ex: Show all the spoils by valiant kings achieved.

senses.d: To end or finish (something); to terminate; (specifically, military) to win (a battle or war).
ex: Full many Countreyes they did ouerronne, / From the vpriſing to the ſetting Sunne, / And many hard aduentures did atchieue; […]
I had novv atchiev'd this rare adventure, ultimately much more to my ſatisfaction than I had beſpoke the nature of it to turn out, […]

senses.d: To attain a goal; to succeed in something, now especially in academic performance; (generally) to make an effort; strive.
ex: He could really achieve in school if he worked hard.
[He] Fights Dragon-like, and does atcheeue as ſoone / As dravv his Svvord: […]

senses.d: Followed by to: to attain a certain position, status, etc.
To come to an end; conclude, end; also, to result, to turn out; or (uncommon) to be affected by fate in a certain way.

grp.label: (transitive) to carry out or conclude (something, as a task) successfully — see also realize
(transitive) to gain or obtain (a desired objective, result, etc.) through effort or skill

From Middle French real (“actual”) + -iser, from Old French reel, from Latin reālis, from rēs (“thing, event, deed, fact”).
Inherited from Latin portāre (“to bring, carry”), from Proto-Indo-European *per- (“go, traverse”).
